messages.content: I want to design a network diagnosis system that separates concurrent causal faults from downstream symptoms under asymmetric routing and incomplete telemetry. It needs to achieve at least 90% fault-localization precision at at least 80% incident coverage with 30% telemetry loss. When fault sets are observationally indistinguishable, it should report that ambiguity rather than assert an unsupported single cause.

The central challenge is to distinguish what is causing an incident from what is merely observed because of those causes, without assuming there can be only one causal fault. Asymmetric routing matters because evidence from one direction cannot automatically stand in for evidence from the other. Incomplete telemetry adds a second constraint: a missing observation is not, by itself, proof that an event did not occur.

The performance target has two simultaneous parts under the stated 30% telemetry-loss condition: at least 90% fault-localization precision and at least 80% incident coverage. The reporting rule also matters independently of those numbers. If the available observations support multiple fault sets equally, the system should say which sets remain indistinguishable, not select one as though the evidence resolved the choice.
What does it mean to separate concurrent causal faults from downstream symptoms? I don't want the design to assume that every observed problem is a separate root fault.

It means allowing more than one fault to be causally relevant while avoiding the opposite mistake of promoting every resulting observation into an independent cause. A symptom may be evidence about a fault without itself being another fault to localize. Equally, evidence that is consistent with one causal fault does not rule out an additional concurrent fault.

At a conceptual level, the diagnosis should distinguish its causal claims from the observations used to support them. That distinction leaves room to say, for example, that two candidate faults could be concurrent, that one observation is downstream of a candidate fault, or that the evidence does not resolve which explanation applies. Those are different claims, and they should not be collapsed into a single-cause account.
How does asymmetric routing affect that reasoning?

It limits what can be inferred by treating opposite directions as interchangeable. Under asymmetric routing, an observation associated with one direction need not describe the conditions encountered in the other direction. A diagnostic explanation should therefore not depend on an unstated assumption that both directions followed the same path.

This matters for both localization and ambiguity. Apparent differences between observations might be compatible with route asymmetry rather than indicating separate faults; conversely, treating the directions as identical could hide a relevant causal distinction. The point is to keep those possibilities separate until the available evidence distinguishes them.
And with 30% telemetry loss, how should I think about missing evidence?

The 30% telemetry loss is the condition under which the precision and coverage targets must hold. It does not mean that 30% of incidents are absent, nor does it specify which observations are missing in a particular incident.

For diagnosis, missing telemetry creates uncertainty rather than a negative finding. If an explanation would have been testable using an observation that is unavailable, the system should not act as if the unavailable observation contradicted that explanation. It can still use the evidence that remains, but the strength and specificity of its claim should reflect what that evidence can actually distinguish.
Could the system still localize a fault when some telemetry is missing?

Yes, in principle. Incomplete telemetry does not make every incident unlocalizable. The question is whether the observations that remain distinguish the relevant causal faults from downstream symptoms and from other candidate fault sets. Sometimes they may support a specific localization; sometimes they may only narrow the possibilities to a set.

That distinction is important for the target. The aim is not to force a uniquely named fault in every incident to raise coverage. It is to attain at least 80% incident coverage while maintaining at least 90% fault-localization precision under 30% telemetry loss, and to represent unresolved ambiguity honestly.
What exactly would count as an observationally indistinguishable fault set?

Consider two candidate explanations, each expressed as a set of causal faults. They are observationally indistinguishable if the available observations do not separate them: on that evidence, choosing one set over the other would require an assumption not established by the observations. This can arise whether a candidate set contains one fault or multiple concurrent faults.

The phrase is about the evidence available for the incident, not a claim that the underlying faults are identical. It also need not imply that no further evidence could ever distinguish them. The report should preserve the distinction between what may actually have happened and what can be inferred from the telemetry at hand.
So if one candidate is a single fault and another is two concurrent faults, the system shouldn't automatically prefer the simpler story?

Correct. Simplicity alone would not justify asserting the single fault if both candidate fault sets are observationally indistinguishable. The system may describe the unresolved alternatives, including that one involves concurrent faults, without claiming to know which is the actual cause.

This does not require treating every imaginable alternative as equally plausible. It requires avoiding a specific unsupported step: turning an unresolved comparison between fault sets into a definitive single-cause explanation.
Would reporting several possibilities undermine fault-localization precision?

Not necessarily, but the evaluation would need to be clear about what a localization claim is. A report that identifies an indistinguishable set of alternatives is different from a report that asserts each alternative occurred, and different again from a report that names one fault as certain. Those outputs should not be conflated when assessing precision.

The stated requirement fixes the target—at least 90% fault-localization precision at at least 80% incident coverage with 30% telemetry loss—but does not specify how ambiguous-set reports are scored. Whatever scoring convention is used, it should not reward an unsupported unique-cause assertion merely because it is more specific.
Is incident coverage the same as saying the system always gives a precise answer?

No. Incident coverage concerns how many incidents receive a qualifying diagnostic output; precision concerns the correctness of localization claims. The exact criteria for a qualifying output are not specified here, so coverage should not be equated with either a response to every incident or a uniquely identified fault for every incident.

The two thresholds must be considered together. Reaching at least 80% incident coverage is not enough if fault-localization precision falls below 90%, and a highly precise result on too few incidents does not by itself meet the coverage target. Both thresholds apply under 30% telemetry loss.
I also want to avoid mistaking a downstream symptom for evidence of another simultaneous fault. Is that just a matter of terminology?

No. The distinction affects the diagnosis itself. If a downstream symptom is counted as an additional causal fault, the reported fault set can be wrong even when the symptom was genuinely observed. Conversely, dismissing a genuinely concurrent causal fault as merely a symptom would leave the causal account incomplete.

The report therefore needs to be careful about the status of each claim: an observed condition, a proposed causal fault, and a downstream consequence are not interchangeable labels. The available evidence may support some of those relationships strongly and leave others unresolved.
Could an asymmetric route and missing telemetry together make that distinction harder?

Yes. Asymmetric routing can limit the relevance of observations from one direction to the other, while missing telemetry removes potential evidence that might distinguish a causal fault from a downstream effect. Together, they can leave more than one causal account consistent with what was observed.

That is a reason to calibrate the conclusion to the evidence, not a reason to abandon localization altogether. Where the remaining observations distinguish concurrent causal faults from symptoms, the system can report that distinction. Where they do not distinguish candidate fault sets, it should report the ambiguity rather than manufacture certainty.
What should the system say when it can narrow an incident down but cannot choose between the remaining fault sets?

It should state the supported scope of the localization and identify the fault sets that remain observationally indistinguishable. It should avoid wording that quietly converts one of those sets into the asserted cause. It can also make clear that the uncertainty is about choosing among causal explanations, not about whether the reported observations exist.

For an abstract illustration, if the available evidence cannot distinguish candidate fault set A from candidate fault set B, the appropriate claim is that A and B remain possible on that evidence. The inappropriate claim is that A alone caused the incident merely because the output format favors one answer. No particular faults, routes, or telemetry sources are implied by that illustration.
I want the target to be demanding without encouraging overconfident answers. What's the principle tying it together?

Localize as specifically as the evidence permits, while preserving uncertainty that the evidence cannot resolve. That principle applies to all parts of the goal: keep concurrent causal faults distinct from downstream symptoms; do not assume symmetric paths under asymmetric routing; do not turn telemetry gaps into proof of absence; and report observationally indistinguishable fault sets instead of an unsupported single cause.

The quantitative requirement remains at least 90% fault-localization precision at at least 80% incident coverage with 30% telemetry loss. Meeting those numbers should reflect accurate, appropriately qualified localization—not a larger number of confident-looking answers obtained by concealing ambiguity.

For the diagnosis system, I propose building asymmetric-path causal factor graphs with missingness-aware telemetry likelihoods and multi-fault inference. The graphs would separate downstream symptoms from causal faults, and the system would return indistinguishable fault sets when the observations cannot resolve them. Does that fit the problem?

Yes. That is a coherent proposed approach to the problem, rather than a claim that the performance targets have already been met. The causal factor graphs provide a way to represent relationships among candidate faults, their possible downstream effects, routing, and telemetry. Representing paths asymmetrically avoids silently treating evidence from one direction as evidence about an identical reverse path.

Missingness-aware telemetry likelihoods address the fact that some observations will be unavailable. Multi-fault inference allows an explanation to contain concurrent causal faults without requiring every observed symptom to become another fault. Finally, returning indistinguishable fault sets makes the output reflect the limits of the available evidence.
Why specify asymmetric-path graphs rather than just causal factor graphs?

Because an otherwise useful causal graph could still embed a misleading symmetry assumption. If it treats the two directions of communication as though they necessarily traverse the same path, it may attribute an observation to the wrong part of a causal explanation or incorrectly combine evidence that does not apply to the same path.

“Asymmetric-path” makes the constraint explicit: the model must allow the relevant paths, and therefore the observations associated with them, to differ by direction. It does not assert that every route differs, nor does it specify any particular route. It prevents symmetry from being assumed where the evidence has not established it.
What is the factor graph doing here? I don't want the name of the method to stand in for the actual reasoning.

Its role is to express a structured causal explanation and how that explanation relates to observations. Conceptually, candidate causal faults can account for downstream effects, while telemetry provides incomplete evidence about those effects. The graph makes those relationships explicit enough to compare fault-set explanations rather than treating each observation as an isolated diagnosis.

The graph is not itself proof that a modeled causal relationship holds. Its usefulness depends on whether the represented relationships and telemetry likelihoods are appropriate. The proposal is to use it as the framework for inference, not to treat the diagram as a substitute for evidence.
Can it represent two causal faults at once without labeling every symptom as a third fault?

That is precisely what the multi-fault and causal aspects are meant to allow. An explanation can include more than one concurrent fault, while an observation caused downstream of those faults can remain an observation or symptom. There is no need to equate “something abnormal was seen” with “another independent causal fault occurred.”

The converse also matters: the model should not force a genuinely separate candidate fault to be described as a downstream symptom simply to keep the explanation singular. Inference compares these possibilities against the available telemetry; the proposal does not presume in advance that one fault or multiple faults must be the answer.
How do missingness-aware telemetry likelihoods help with that comparison?

They make the relationship between an explanation and the available observations account for telemetry that is absent. Without that distinction, the system could mistakenly treat an unobserved signal as a normal reading, a contradictory reading, or proof that an expected effect did not happen.

A missingness-aware likelihood should keep “no observation was available” distinct from “an observation was available and had this value.” That lets the inference draw on what was actually observed while remaining appropriately uncertain where telemetry could have distinguished a causal fault from a symptom, or one fault set from another, but is unavailable.
Does ‘missingness-aware’ mean assuming why the telemetry went missing?

No particular cause of missingness is established by the proposal. Being aware of missingness means that the likelihood treatment does not silently replace unavailable telemetry with an observed value or interpret its absence as proof of a network fault.

If the reason for missing telemetry is unknown, the diagnosis should not invent one. The model can acknowledge that observations are unavailable and that this limits what can be distinguished. The proposal does not specify a particular missingness mechanism or claim that missing telemetry is always uninformative.
Suppose the remaining observations are compatible with either one fault or two concurrent faults. Would multi-fault inference itself decide which is right?

It should make both kinds of explanation representable and comparable, but its ability to choose between them depends on the evidence. If the available observations do not distinguish the single-fault set from the two-fault set, permitting multi-fault inference does not create information that was never observed.

In that situation, the proposed output is the indistinguishable fault sets, not a definitive selection of the single-fault explanation or an unsupported assertion that both faults occurred. “Multi-fault” describes what the inference can consider; it is not an instruction to prefer more faults.
I want to be careful with the word ‘sets.’ Are those alternative diagnoses, or a list of faults the system says all occurred?

Those are different meanings, so the output needs to preserve the distinction. Within a candidate fault set, its members are proposed as concurrent causal faults. If several candidate sets are observationally indistinguishable, those sets are alternatives that the available observations do not resolve.

Returning two alternative sets is therefore not the same as asserting the union of all their members occurred. It is also not the same as asserting just one member from a set containing multiple faults. Keeping those levels separate is essential to reporting ambiguity honestly.
Could the graph mistake a downstream symptom for a separate fault just because it is closely associated with the incident?

That is a risk the design is intended to address, not something the use of a graph automatically eliminates. A symptom can be strongly associated with an incident while still being an effect rather than an additional cause. The causal structure should distinguish the proposed direction of explanation from mere co-occurrence, and the inference should not count an observed effect as an extra fault simply because it is abnormal.

If the evidence does not resolve whether a particular finding is a downstream effect or indicates another concurrent fault, the output should reflect that uncertainty. A formal representation is useful partly because it makes the competing interpretations visible.
What happens if asymmetric routing changes which observations are relevant to a candidate fault set?

The candidate explanation should be assessed against observations in light of the paths to which those observations pertain. Evidence associated with one direction should not be transferred to another direction on the unexamined assumption that their paths coincide.

This is why the path representation and the causal relationships belong in the same proposal. Path asymmetry affects what a candidate fault could explain, and the telemetry likelihoods affect how strongly the available observations support that explanation. Neither element can safely be ignored while comparing fault sets.
Would a missing observation from one direction be grounds to rule out a fault on that direction?

Not on its own. A missing observation is not an observed absence of an effect. The missingness-aware treatment should prevent the inference from ruling out a candidate merely because telemetry that might have supported it was unavailable.

That does not mean every candidate survives regardless of the evidence. Actual observations may distinguish candidates. The point is to separate those observations from gaps in telemetry, especially when path asymmetry means evidence from a different direction cannot automatically fill the gap.
Is ‘observationally indistinguishable’ a statement that the candidate fault sets really are the same?

No. The candidate sets may describe genuinely different causal situations. They are observationally indistinguishable when the telemetry available for the incident does not provide a supported basis for choosing among them. The limitation is in what can be inferred from the observations, not necessarily in the underlying situations.

Nor should the term require pretending that the system has proved no possible future observation could distinguish them. The proposed report concerns the evidence at hand.
Does the proposal require exact equality between numerical likelihoods before it can return indistinguishable fault sets?

No exact-equality rule is specified. The important reporting constraint is epistemic: do not convert a distinction the observations cannot support into a definitive single-cause claim. The likelihoods are part of comparing explanations, but a numerical output should not be treated as permission to assert that the evidence uniquely identifies a fault set when it does not.

How to operationalize that reporting judgment is not settled in this proposal. What is settled in the proposal is the intended behavior: preserve observationally unresolved alternatives.
Could reporting ambiguity make the diagnosis system sound less useful?

It can make a report less specific, but appropriately so. A set of unresolved alternatives still communicates which causal fault sets are under consideration and which distinction the observations cannot establish. That is more informative than an unsupported single-cause explanation that conceals uncertainty.

The proposal aims to be specific when the available telemetry supports specificity, and explicit about indistinguishable fault sets when it does not. Missingness-aware inference and asymmetric-path reasoning are meant to help draw that boundary accurately, not to make every report ambiguous.
How do these pieces fit with the precision and coverage requirements we discussed?

They are proposed means of pursuing those requirements, not evidence that they are already satisfied. Multi-fault inference and symptom separation aim to improve the correctness of fault-localization claims. Asymmetric-path modeling aims to avoid misleading path assumptions. Missingness-aware likelihoods aim to keep inference meaningful when telemetry is incomplete. Reporting indistinguishable fault sets aims to avoid false specificity.

The required performance remains at least 90% fault-localization precision at at least 80% incident coverage with 30% telemetry loss. This proposal does not by itself establish that either threshold is achieved; it describes how the diagnosis and its uncertainty would be represented.
So the output should be able to say more than just ‘fault found’ or ‘no fault found’?

Yes. The proposed inference may support a particular causal fault set, or it may leave multiple fault sets observationally indistinguishable. In either case, it should keep downstream symptoms distinct from the causal faults it reports.

That does not commit to a particular output format. The substantive requirement is that a reader can tell what is asserted as a causal explanation, what is treated as a downstream symptom, and where the available observations leave alternatives unresolved.
I don't want the factor graph to imply that every telemetry signal has a simple one-to-one fault explanation.

It need not imply that. The point of a causal factor graph with multi-fault inference is to represent relationships among possible causes, effects, and observations without requiring one observed signal to correspond to exactly one fault. A symptom might be compatible with several candidate fault sets, and several observations might bear on the same causal explanation.

Where those relationships do not distinguish the candidates—particularly with asymmetric paths or missing telemetry—the inference should retain the competing fault sets rather than manufacture a one-to-one mapping.
Can you state the proposal in a compact way without making it sound like an accomplished result?

Build asymmetric-path causal factor graphs to relate candidate causal fault sets to downstream symptoms and available observations. Use missingness-aware telemetry likelihoods and multi-fault inference to compare those sets without treating absent telemetry as an observed negative or assuming there is only one cause. When the observations do not distinguish candidate fault sets, return those alternatives rather than assert an unsupported single-cause explanation. This is a proposed design, not a demonstrated performance result.
How can asymmetric-path factor graphs separate concurrent faults from symptoms and flag indistinguishable fault sets under 30% telemetry loss?

They can make three distinctions explicit in the same inference problem: which paths an observation pertains to, which conditions are candidate causes versus downstream effects, and which observations are actually available. The graph can represent a candidate fault set containing more than one concurrent fault, then assess whether that set could account for the observed symptoms along the relevant directional paths.

Under 30% telemetry loss, the unavailable observations must remain unavailable in that assessment—not be treated as normal readings or as contradictions. If the remaining observations cannot distinguish two candidate fault sets, the output should retain both as alternatives rather than turn one into a definitive cause.
Where, in that picture, does the distinction between a fault and a symptom come from?

It comes from the causal relationships the model is proposing, not merely from whether a condition looks abnormal. A candidate fault is part of an explanation for downstream effects; a symptom is an effect the explanation seeks to account for. The factor graph provides a structured way to express and compare those relationships against observations.

It cannot establish causality just by assigning labels to nodes. If an observed condition could be either a downstream effect or evidence of another concurrent fault, both interpretations may need to remain candidates unless the available observations distinguish them.
Does allowing multiple faults make it too easy to explain every symptom by adding another cause?

It creates that possibility if the inference treats every added fault as justified merely because it could explain something. Multi-fault inference should instead allow concurrent faults without requiring them: an added fault is a causal claim that needs support from the available observations and the modeled relationships.

The key comparison is between whole candidate fault sets. If a symptom is already accounted for downstream of a candidate set, its presence alone does not establish an additional fault. If the observations cannot distinguish that set from one containing an additional fault, the answer is an unresolved comparison, not an automatic declaration that the additional fault occurred.
Why compare whole fault sets instead of assessing each candidate fault separately?

Because concurrent causes can affect how the same observations are explained. Assessing each candidate in isolation risks losing the distinction between “these faults could occur together” and “either fault alone could explain what was seen.” It can also encourage a list of individually plausible faults to be mistaken for a claim that all of them occurred.

Comparing sets preserves the structure of the claim. A set proposes concurrent causes; different sets are alternative explanations. That is also the level at which observational indistinguishability matters.
What does making the paths asymmetric add to the comparison?

It keeps evidence tied to the direction and path it actually concerns. Without that distinction, the graph could effectively assume that an observation from one direction describes the reverse direction as well. Under asymmetric routing, that assumption need not hold.

Consequently, a candidate fault set should be assessed through its proposed causal relationship to observations on the relevant paths, rather than through an assumed shared path. This can change which observations bear on a candidate explanation without implying any particular route or fault in advance.
Is the graph saying that the two directions must always differ?

No. It must permit them to differ, not require a difference. “Asymmetric-path” prevents the inference from relying on symmetry without support. If the available evidence does not establish whether the paths coincide, the model should not manufacture that fact either.

The useful distinction is between representing directional paths separately and asserting a specific path arrangement for an incident. The former is part of the proposed method; the latter would require evidence.
How do the telemetry likelihoods interact with the causal graph?

The graph describes which observations could follow from a candidate causal explanation, while telemetry likelihoods express how the available readings bear on that explanation. Their missingness-aware aspect keeps an unavailable reading distinct from a reading that was observed and had a particular value.

Together, those elements let the inference compare candidate fault sets using what was actually observed, while recognizing that some potentially distinguishing evidence is absent. A likelihood can help assess an explanation; it does not, by itself, turn a modeled causal link into an established fact.
With 30% telemetry loss, should the missing readings simply count as weak evidence against every fault set?

No. A missing reading is not a weak negative reading. Treating it as evidence against every set would confuse lack of observation with an observed result. The diagnosis should use the readings that remain and carry forward uncertainty about distinctions the missing readings might have resolved.

The stated 30% loss describes the condition the method must handle; it does not specify which readings are missing in any particular incident. Nor does it establish why they went missing. Those details should not be inferred from the percentage alone.
Could the absence of telemetry itself ever matter to inference?

Potentially, but that depends on what is known about the missingness process. The proposal does not establish such a process, so it would be unsupported to interpret every telemetry gap as a symptom of a network fault—or to declare that missingness could never carry information.

The safe conceptual distinction is to represent what was observed, what was unavailable, and any assumptions needed to interpret that unavailability. Without support for an assumption about why data is missing, the graph should not use the gap as if its cause were known.
How would it flag that two fault sets are indistinguishable, as opposed to merely assigning them different scores?

It would compare what each set implies about the observations that are available. If those observations do not provide a supported basis for choosing between the sets, the report should identify them as unresolved alternatives. That is a statement about the discriminating power of the evidence, not necessarily about exact numerical equality.

The question does not prescribe a numerical rule for making that reporting judgment. A score alone should not be presented as proof of a uniquely identified cause when the underlying observations leave the candidate sets observationally indistinguishable.
If one set has one fault and the other has two, does flagging them mean saying three faults occurred?

No. The members of each set describe faults proposed to occur concurrently within that particular explanation. The sets themselves are alternatives. Reporting both means the available observations do not establish which explanation occurred; it does not assert the union of their members.

That distinction is especially important here, because collapsing the alternatives into one list could falsely assert extra concurrent faults, while choosing only the one-fault set could assert an unsupported single cause.
What if both sets account for the visible symptoms but imply different unobserved downstream effects?

If the effects that would distinguish them are unobserved because telemetry is unavailable, their differing implications do not by themselves resolve the incident. The inference can recognize that the candidate sets make different claims, but it should not act as though the missing observations confirmed or refuted either claim.

Other available observations might still distinguish the sets. If none do, they remain observationally indistinguishable on the evidence at hand, even though the proposed causal situations differ.
Could asymmetric routing make two explanations look indistinguishable when a symmetric model would choose one?

It could reveal that the apparent distinction depended on an unsupported symmetry assumption. If a symmetric model transfers an observation from one direction to the other, it may seem to rule out a candidate that the actual directional evidence does not rule out. Keeping the paths separate prevents that particular inference from being made without support.

That is a conceptual possibility, not a claim about any observed incident or a measured comparison between models. The purpose is to make clear which conclusions follow from available path-specific observations and which would require additional assumptions.
Can the graph determine on its own whether something is a downstream symptom or an independent concurrent fault?

No. It can encode and compare candidate causal accounts, including one in which a condition is downstream and another in which it indicates an independent fault. Whether the evidence favors either account depends on the observations, their relevance to the asymmetric paths, and the credibility of the modeled relationships.

A graph is useful because it exposes those alternatives rather than hiding them in a single label. It should not be treated as a device that creates certainty where the telemetry does not support it.
So is ‘indistinguishable’ just another way of saying the diagnosis has low confidence?

Not quite. Low confidence describes uncertainty about a conclusion in general. Observational indistinguishability identifies a more specific limitation: the available observations cannot discriminate among particular candidate fault sets. Those sets might each be coherent explanations, yet the evidence lacks a basis for selecting one.

A useful report would preserve that structure. Saying only “low confidence” could conceal which alternatives remain unresolved, whereas asserting one cause would conceal the uncertainty altogether.
Give me the reasoning sequence, but keep it conceptual rather than prescribing implementation details.

First, represent candidate causal faults, potential downstream symptoms, and the observations relevant to directional paths without assuming the paths are symmetric. Second, allow inference over fault sets, including sets with concurrent faults, so the explanation is not forced into a single-cause form. Third, assess those explanations using the available telemetry while treating missing readings as missing.

Then compare what the remaining evidence can actually distinguish. Where it supports a causal distinction, the diagnosis can express it; where different fault sets remain observationally indistinguishable, the report should present them as alternatives. Throughout, an observed symptom should not become an extra causal fault solely because it is abnormal.
Does that sequence guarantee correct separation under 30% telemetry loss?

No. It describes how an asymmetric-path factor-graph approach could reason about concurrent faults, symptoms, and indistinguishable sets under that loss condition. Its correctness would still depend on whether the causal relationships and telemetry likelihoods adequately reflect the situation, as well as on what evidence remains available.

Thirty percent telemetry loss makes the distinction harder; the method cannot recover information that the remaining observations do not contain. Its essential safeguard is to make supported distinctions when possible and flag unresolved fault sets rather than fill the gaps with an unsupported single-cause explanation.

Here's the hypothesis I want to examine: under 30% telemetry loss, asymmetric-path multi-fault inference achieves at least 90% localization precision at at least 80% coverage, grouping indistinguishable faults while excluding symptoms. Am I stating the claim carefully enough?

Yes, provided it remains explicitly a hypothesis rather than a reported result. It makes a joint performance claim under a specified condition: with 30% telemetry loss, localization precision is at least 90% while coverage is at least 80%. It also claims a particular diagnostic behavior: faults that cannot be distinguished from the available observations are grouped as unresolved alternatives, while downstream symptoms are excluded from the causal fault output.

Those behavioral claims matter alongside the numbers. A system would not satisfy the intended hypothesis merely by producing precise-looking labels if it conflated symptoms with faults or concealed indistinguishable explanations.
Does ‘at least 90% precision at at least 80% coverage’ mean I can state the two thresholds separately?

You can describe them separately to explain what each measures, but the hypothesis requires them together under the same stated 30% telemetry-loss condition. Achieving the precision threshold while falling short of the coverage threshold would not establish the full claim; neither would achieving coverage while falling short of precision.

The wording also does not say that precision must be exactly 90% or coverage exactly 80%. Those are minimum thresholds.
I don't want ‘grouping indistinguishable faults’ to sound like it declares all grouped faults occurred. How should we read it?

Read it as retaining ambiguity among fault possibilities the available observations cannot distinguish. Where the diagnosis is expressed in fault sets, members within one candidate set are proposed concurrent faults, while different indistinguishable sets are alternative explanations. Reporting the alternatives does not assert that every fault appearing in every alternative occurred.

That distinction protects the hypothesis from being interpreted as indiscriminately collecting possible faults into one causal claim. The grouping is a way of representing an unresolved inference, not a claim of simultaneous occurrence across all alternatives.
What exactly does ‘excluding symptoms’ assert? Does it mean symptoms should disappear from the diagnosis entirely?

No. It means downstream symptoms should not be reported as though they were causal faults. A symptom can remain part of the observations or part of the explanation of what follows from a candidate fault set; excluding it from the localized fault set does not require hiding it.

The distinction is especially important when faults can be concurrent. The inference should permit more than one genuine causal fault without turning every resulting abnormal observation into yet another fault.
Could the hypothesis still hold if the system often says it cannot distinguish between candidate fault sets?

Possibly, but the hypothesis does not specify how such outputs count toward localization precision or coverage. It does require grouping indistinguishable faults rather than pretending the observations identify a unique cause. How often that situation occurs, and whether the joint numerical thresholds are met, cannot be inferred from the hypothesis alone.

The key is not to improve apparent specificity by asserting one fault set when the evidence leaves alternatives unresolved. That would conflict with the stated diagnostic behavior even if the output looked decisive.
Does the 30% telemetry loss imply the system knows which missing readings would have resolved each case?

No. The percentage specifies the loss condition for the hypothesis, not the identity, significance, or reason for missing observations in any particular incident. The inference must not treat an unavailable reading as if it were an observed absence of a symptom.

It may be possible to recognize that the remaining evidence does not distinguish candidate fault sets without knowing what the missing readings would have shown. The hypothesis does not claim to recover information that was never observed.
Why is asymmetric-path reasoning part of a performance hypothesis about fault localization?

Because path direction affects which observations can bear on a candidate explanation. The proposed inference does not assume that evidence from one direction describes an identical reverse path. That is relevant to deciding whether observations support concurrent causal faults, downstream symptoms, or several unresolved fault sets.

The hypothesis is that this kind of inference attains the stated precision and coverage under 30% telemetry loss. It is not itself evidence that allowing asymmetric paths produces those numbers, nor does it assert that the two directions differ in every incident.
And what work is ‘multi-fault’ doing in the hypothesis?

It allows the diagnosis to consider concurrent causal faults rather than forcing every incident into a one-cause explanation. The term does not mean that multiple faults must be reported for every incident, or that a symptom becomes a fault whenever it is abnormal.

That flexibility is paired with the ambiguity rule. If available observations cannot distinguish a single-fault explanation from a concurrent-fault explanation, the hypothesis calls for an honest grouping of unresolved alternatives, not an unsupported choice of either one.
If a symptom is wrongly included in a fault set, would that matter even if the system also identifies a real fault?

Yes. The claim specifically includes excluding symptoms from causal fault localization. Identifying a genuine fault does not make it accurate to report a downstream effect as an additional causal fault. Such an output would blur precisely the distinction the hypothesis is meant to preserve.

Likewise, excluding symptoms should not become a pretext for suppressing a second fault when the evidence supports concurrent causes. Both errors concern what the localized fault set actually asserts.
Can you distinguish what is being predicted from what is already known here?

The prediction is that asymmetric-path multi-fault inference, under 30% telemetry loss, reaches at least 90% localization precision at at least 80% coverage while grouping observationally indistinguishable faults and excluding downstream symptoms from the causal fault output. Nothing in that formulation establishes that the thresholds have been reached or that the separation succeeds in any observed incident.

The terms explain what the hypothesis claims; they do not supply results. Any statement that it has achieved the predicted performance would go beyond the hypothesis.
Is it accurate to say the hypothesis predicts perfect identification whenever the system covers an incident?

No. At least 90% localization precision is not perfect precision, and coverage of at least 80% is not a claim about every incident. Moreover, an incident might leave fault sets indistinguishable; the hypothesis expects that uncertainty to be represented rather than replaced with a uniquely identified cause.

It also does not define the exact scoring treatment of an ambiguity report. The numerical thresholds and the requirement for honest grouping should be kept distinct rather than assuming that a grouped output is automatically a uniquely correct localization.
Does grouping indistinguishable faults mean the inference must give up on distinguishing any faults whenever telemetry is missing?

No. Telemetry loss does not make all candidate explanations equally supported. Available observations may still distinguish some fault sets or show that a condition is downstream of a fault rather than an independent cause.

Grouping applies where the observations do not support a distinction. The hypothesis does not call for blanket uncertainty; it calls for localization when supported and explicit ambiguity where a stronger claim would be unwarranted.
Could I shorten the hypothesis to ‘it localizes faults despite missing data’?

That would lose important parts of the claim. It would omit the 30% telemetry-loss condition, the simultaneous thresholds of at least 90% localization precision and at least 80% coverage, the asymmetric-path and multi-fault character of the inference, and the distinction between grouping indistinguishable faults and excluding symptoms.

A shorter formulation can still preserve those essentials: ‘Under 30% telemetry loss, asymmetric-path multi-fault inference is hypothesized to reach ≥90% localization precision at ≥80% coverage, grouping observationally indistinguishable fault alternatives while excluding downstream symptoms from causal fault sets.’
What if several faults are genuinely concurrent but the available observations cannot tell which combination occurred?

That is compatible with the kind of uncertainty the hypothesis addresses. The inference can consider combinations of concurrent faults as candidate sets. If the remaining observations do not distinguish among those sets, it should report the unresolved alternatives instead of asserting one particular combination.

The fact that some alternatives include multiple faults does not turn their shared downstream symptoms into faults. Nor does the existence of uncertainty justify collapsing all candidate combinations into a claim that every mentioned fault occurred.
So the hypothesis includes a restraint on what the system says, not just a prediction about two percentages?

Exactly. The two percentages are the performance prediction under 30% telemetry loss. Grouping indistinguishable faults and excluding symptoms describe the kind of localization the hypothesis predicts. They constrain how an output represents causal faults and uncertainty, so a numerically attractive answer based on unsupported single-cause assertions would not express the full hypothesis.

To evaluate the hypothesis, I want to simulate 10,000 AsymRouteBench incidents with concurrent faults, asymmetric paths, and 30% telemetry loss, then measure precision, coverage, ambiguity, and symptom rejection. How should I describe this activity without implying it has already happened?

Describe it as a planned simulation and measurement: simulate 10,000 AsymRouteBench incidents under those conditions, then assess the four named outcomes. That states the intended activity without claiming that incidents have been generated or results obtained.

The measurements address different parts of the diagnostic claim. Precision and coverage concern localization performance; ambiguity concerns whether unresolved fault sets are represented honestly; and symptom rejection concerns whether downstream symptoms are kept out of causal fault reports.
Why measure ambiguity separately from precision?

Because a diagnosis can be wrong in how it represents uncertainty even if its output contains a plausible fault. The ambiguity measure should speak to whether the system flags fault sets that the available observations cannot distinguish, rather than asserting one as uniquely established.

Precision addresses the accuracy of localization claims. The two are related, but neither automatically establishes the other. The activity does not yet specify a scoring rule for ambiguous outputs, so the measures should remain distinct rather than silently treating every reported alternative as an asserted fault.
And why isn't symptom rejection just another name for precision?

Symptom rejection focuses on a particular error: reporting a downstream effect as though it were a causal fault. A general precision measure may reflect erroneous localization claims, but a separate symptom-rejection measure makes that specific distinction visible.

It also helps keep two questions apart: whether the system identifies causal faults accurately, and whether it avoids adding observed symptoms to the fault set. Measuring both is consistent with allowing genuinely concurrent faults.
Should I say the simulation proves the approach meets at least 90% localization precision at at least 80% coverage?

Not before the simulation and measurements take place. The planned activity would provide a way to assess the hypothesis under 30% telemetry loss. The thresholds—at least 90% localization precision and at least 80% coverage—are what the resulting measurements would be compared against, not results supplied by the plan.

Even once measurements exist, the claims should match what they actually show. For now, it is accurate to say that the 10,000-incident AsymRouteBench simulation is intended to evaluate those thresholds and the ambiguity and symptom-rejection behavior.
What role do the concurrent faults play in the simulated incidents?

They make the activity relevant to whether inference can represent more than one causal fault without mistaking downstream symptoms for additional causes. The diagnosis may need to distinguish an explanation containing concurrent faults from other candidate fault sets.

The activity states that the AsymRouteBench incidents involve concurrent faults; it does not specify particular faults, how often any combination appears, or what observations each combination produces. Those details need not be invented to explain what is being evaluated.
Why include asymmetric paths explicitly in the simulation description?

Because the diagnostic question concerns evidence whose relevance can differ by path direction. Including asymmetric paths makes that condition part of the evaluation activity rather than leaving it as an untested assumption.

It does not specify particular routes or say that every directional difference has the same effect. It says the simulated incidents should exercise the asymmetric-path condition while the measurements assess how the proposed inference behaves.
Is 30% telemetry loss a result to measure, or a condition of the activity?

Here it is a specified condition: simulate the 10,000 incidents with 30% telemetry loss, then measure precision, coverage, ambiguity, and symptom rejection under that condition. The statement does not say which telemetry is lost in each incident or why it is missing.

That distinction matters because an unavailable observation should not be interpreted as an observed negative merely because the loss percentage is known.
When measuring coverage, should every ambiguous report count as a successful localization?

The activity does not prescribe that scoring rule. An ambiguous report can convey a meaningful restriction on possible fault sets, but whether it counts toward coverage depends on what qualifies as a covered incident. It should not be counted as a uniquely resolved localization if it does not make one.

Whatever convention is used to interpret the coverage measurement, it should keep an honest report of unresolved alternatives distinct from a definitive fault claim. Otherwise, the coverage figure could obscure the ambiguity the activity is explicitly meant to measure.
Could I measure ambiguity by counting every time the system returns more than one fault?

That would conflate two different things. More than one fault within a single candidate set represents a proposed concurrent-fault explanation. More than one observationally indistinguishable candidate set represents unresolved alternatives. Ambiguity concerns the latter distinction, not simply the number of faults named.

The activity calls for measuring ambiguity, but it does not define a particular formula. Its interpretation should preserve the difference between concurrent faults and competing fault sets.
What should symptom rejection tell me that an ambiguity measurement wouldn't?

It should tell you whether downstream symptoms are excluded from the reported causal faults. A system could faithfully flag several indistinguishable fault sets yet still mistakenly include a symptom as a causal member of those sets. Conversely, it could avoid labeling symptoms as faults while asserting an unjustifiably unique explanation.

Measuring both avoids treating uncertainty reporting and cause-versus-symptom separation as the same behavior.
Does the activity assume that missing telemetry will always make fault sets indistinguishable?

No. Thirty percent telemetry loss can remove potentially distinguishing observations, but the evidence that remains may still distinguish some fault sets. Ambiguity should be measured rather than presumed.

The converse also matters: the plan should not presume that any particular unresolved comparison is resolved simply because the inference returns a preferred output. The ambiguity measurement is there to examine whether the report reflects what the available observations can support.
If the system returns a single fault set, does that automatically mean it has rejected symptoms correctly?

No. A single returned set could still contain a downstream symptom misclassified as a causal fault. That is why symptom rejection warrants its own measurement.

Likewise, returning a set with multiple faults is not by itself a symptom-rejection failure: the faults may be concurrent causes. The distinction depends on causal status, not on whether the reported set has one member or several.
How do I avoid overstating what a simulation of 10,000 incidents would establish?

Keep the claim tied to the planned AsymRouteBench activity and its stated conditions. The number 10,000 specifies the proposed simulation size; it does not supply a precision estimate, coverage figure, ambiguity result, or symptom-rejection result. Nor does the plan alone establish how conclusions would extend beyond those simulated incidents.

For now, say that the activity will measure those outcomes under concurrent faults, asymmetric paths, and 30% telemetry loss. Do not describe the hypothesis as confirmed on the strength of an activity that has only been proposed.
Is the purpose to evaluate only the two numerical thresholds?

No. Precision and coverage address the numerical performance claim, including the at-least-90% precision and at-least-80% coverage thresholds under 30% telemetry loss. Ambiguity and symptom rejection address whether the diagnosis represents indistinguishable fault sets and separates downstream symptoms from causal faults.

All four measurements belong in the activity description. Meeting a numerical threshold would not, by itself, describe how well the system handles unresolved alternatives or symptom misclassification.
Can you restate the activity as one careful sentence?

Plan to simulate 10,000 AsymRouteBench incidents involving concurrent faults and asymmetric paths with 30% telemetry loss, and measure localization precision, incident coverage, ambiguity reporting, and rejection of downstream symptoms as causal faults.

The AsymRouteBench results are in: under 30% telemetry loss, localization precision was 92% at 83% coverage. Symptom rejection was 94%, and indistinguishable cases returned fault sets. How should I present that evidence?

Present the precision and coverage together: AsymRouteBench recorded 92% localization precision at 83% coverage under 30% telemetry loss. Then report the other two findings separately: 94% symptom rejection, and fault-set outputs for indistinguishable cases. Keeping those statements separate makes clear what each result measures without implying that one percentage captures every aspect of the diagnosis.
Why keep ‘at 83% coverage’ attached to the precision figure?

Because the reported precision is associated with that level of coverage. Saying only “92% localization precision” would omit how broadly the system produced the localization outputs being described. Conversely, “83% coverage” alone would say nothing about their precision.

The evidence gives the pair—92% precision at 83% coverage—under the same 30% telemetry-loss condition. It does not provide precision at other coverage levels.
Does 94% symptom rejection mean symptoms never appeared in the reported faults?

No. The reported symptom-rejection value is 94%, not 100%. It indicates how the system performed on that measure in AsymRouteBench; it does not justify saying that downstream symptoms were always excluded from causal fault outputs.

The evidence also does not specify which symptoms were rejected or how individual cases were classified, so a case-by-case account would go beyond the reported result.
What can I say about the indistinguishable cases?

You can say that indistinguishable cases returned fault sets. That reports the observed output behavior without turning an unresolved diagnosis into a uniquely identified cause.

The result does not state how many such cases there were, how large the returned sets were, or whether every member or alternative in every set was correct. Those details should not be inferred from the fact that fault sets were returned.
Could ‘returned fault sets’ be mistaken for saying every fault named in those outputs occurred?

Yes, so it helps to describe them as outputs for cases the observations could not distinguish. A candidate set can describe faults proposed to occur together; multiple candidate sets can represent alternative explanations. Reporting such sets is not, by itself, a claim that the union of all faults appearing across the alternatives occurred.

The AsymRouteBench finding is about the form of the output in indistinguishable cases. It should not be paraphrased as certainty about every fault named in those outputs.
Do these numbers tell us how many indistinguishable incidents there were?

No. The stated evidence provides localization precision, coverage, symptom rejection, and the fact that indistinguishable cases returned fault sets. It does not give a count or percentage of indistinguishable cases. Neither 83% coverage nor 94% symptom rejection can be used as a substitute for that missing quantity.
Is it fair to describe the results as having separated every concurrent fault from every downstream symptom?

No. The 94% symptom-rejection figure does not establish perfect symptom separation, and the other reported figures do not establish case-by-case correctness for every concurrent-fault explanation. A faithful description reports the measured values and the fault-set behavior without expanding them into an all-incidents claim.
Should I phrase 30% telemetry loss as a finding about why observations were missing?

No. It is the condition under which these AsymRouteBench results are reported. The evidence does not identify why particular telemetry was unavailable or say which missing observations affected particular diagnoses. “Under 30% telemetry loss” preserves the condition without inventing a missingness explanation.
Does the evidence show whether the fault sets for indistinguishable cases were narrow or broad?

It does not. Returning fault sets tells us that those cases received a set-based output, but not how many candidate faults or alternative sets an output contained. Describing the outputs as narrowly localized, exhaustive, or uniformly sized would require information not included in these results.
What if I say the benchmark had 92% precision, 83% coverage, and 94% accuracy at rejecting symptoms?

That conveys the three reported values, but I would retain the original metric names to avoid changing their meaning: 92% localization precision at 83% coverage under 30% telemetry loss, and 94% symptom rejection. “Accuracy at rejecting symptoms” might be read as a different metric unless its definition is supplied. Add separately that indistinguishable cases returned fault sets.
Can the 92% localization precision figure tell me whether the system handled ambiguity correctly?

Not by itself. The precision figure concerns localization claims at the reported coverage. The separate finding about indistinguishable cases tells us that those cases returned fault sets, but the evidence does not provide a numerical ambiguity measure or specify how such outputs were scored in the precision calculation.

It is therefore better to report the precision figure and the indistinguishable-case behavior side by side, rather than claim that one proves every aspect of the other.
Give me a concise statement that keeps all four findings and their limits intact.

In AsymRouteBench, under 30% telemetry loss, localization precision was 92% at 83% coverage, symptom rejection was 94%, and indistinguishable cases returned fault sets. These results do not specify how many cases were indistinguishable or establish perfect symptom rejection.

I want to adopt missingness-aware multi-fault factor graphs with ambiguity-set outputs. The reason is that AsymRouteBench exceeds the precision and coverage targets under 30% telemetry loss. Is that an accurate statement of the decision?

Yes. The decision is to adopt missingness-aware multi-fault factor graphs and have them return ambiguity sets when the available observations do not distinguish candidate fault sets. The stated basis is that AsymRouteBench exceeded both the localization-precision and incident-coverage targets under 30% telemetry loss.

That is a decision grounded in the reported benchmark performance, not a claim that every incident will have a unique or correct diagnosis.
Can I be explicit about what ‘exceeds’ means here?

Yes. AsymRouteBench reported 92% localization precision at 83% coverage under 30% telemetry loss. Those figures are above the respective targets of at least 90% precision and at least 80% coverage. Keeping precision attached to its reported coverage level makes the comparison clear without implying a result at some other coverage level.
Does adopting the factor graphs mean we should always return one best fault set?

No. Ambiguity-set outputs are an explicit part of the decision. When the available observations cannot distinguish candidate fault sets, the output should preserve those alternatives rather than present one as uniquely established.

The decision still allows a specific localization when the evidence supports one. It does not require ambiguity in every case, any more than it requires a single answer in every case.
I worry that ‘multi-fault’ and ‘ambiguity set’ will be read as the same thing.

They refer to different aspects of the diagnosis. Multi-fault factor graphs allow a candidate explanation to contain concurrent causal faults. An ambiguity-set output represents alternative candidate explanations that the available observations cannot resolve.

A report of alternatives should not be read as a claim that every fault appearing across them occurred. Nor does a candidate set containing multiple faults necessarily mean the diagnosis is ambiguous: the distinction is between concurrency within an explanation and uncertainty between explanations.
What part of the decision addresses the missing telemetry?

The missingness-aware part. It calls for inference that keeps an unavailable telemetry reading distinct from a reading that was observed and found normal, abnormal, or contradictory. That distinction matters under the stated 30% telemetry-loss condition because missing observations can limit which fault sets the evidence can distinguish.

Adopting that treatment does not assert a particular reason telemetry went missing, and it does not make an unobserved value available to the diagnosis.
Does the benchmark result let me say this decision solves incomplete telemetry generally?

No. The decision cites AsymRouteBench exceeding the precision and coverage targets under 30% telemetry loss. It does not establish the same performance under every loss condition or in every setting. You can state the benchmark result and the resulting adoption decision without extending the measured claim beyond its stated condition.
How should the adopted approach treat downstream symptoms?

It should keep downstream symptoms distinct from the causal faults proposed by a candidate fault set. Multi-fault inference permits more than one cause, but an abnormal observation should not become another cause merely because it is visible alongside those faults.

The ambiguity-set output should preserve that distinction too: unresolved alternatives concern candidate causal fault sets, not a pooled list in which symptoms are silently promoted to faults.
Is 94% symptom rejection part of the reason stated in this decision?

The reason stated in the decision is that AsymRouteBench exceeds the precision and coverage targets under 30% loss. The reported 94% symptom rejection provides separate context about the benchmark, but the decision does not say that symptom rejection reached a specified target or make it an additional threshold for adoption. It also should not be described as perfect rejection.
Should I describe the ambiguity-set output as an admission that the factor graph failed?

No. If the available observations cannot distinguish candidate fault sets, returning the unresolved alternatives is the intended output behavior. It avoids claiming more than the evidence supports. A uniquely worded answer would not become better merely by concealing that ambiguity.

That said, an ambiguity-set output is not proof that every possible alternative has been identified correctly. The decision specifies how unresolved explanations are to be reported; it does not establish perfection in every case.
The diagnosis problem involves asymmetric paths. Does this wording of the decision require me to claim a new result about routing?

No. The decision adopts missingness-aware multi-fault factor graphs with ambiguity-set outputs in the context of the asymmetric-path diagnosis problem. Its stated performance basis is the AsymRouteBench precision and coverage result under 30% telemetry loss. It does not separately claim a measured effect of path asymmetry or establish a result for any particular route.

In describing the approach, you can still explain that directional path evidence should not be treated as interchangeable without support. That explains the diagnosis context without adding a new benchmark finding.
Can the target comparison be made without suggesting the system is perfect?

Yes. Say that the reported 92% localization precision at 83% coverage exceeds the respective minimum targets of 90% and 80% under 30% telemetry loss. Both reported percentages are below 100%, and neither implies that every covered incident was localized correctly or that every incident was covered.

The comparison supports the stated decision while leaving its measured scope intact.
What would be an overconfident way to announce this decision?

Saying that the adopted system always finds the true fault, always rejects symptoms, or uniquely resolves every incident would go beyond the decision and the cited benchmark result. So would saying that the AsymRouteBench figures guarantee the same precision and coverage under conditions other than the reported 30% telemetry loss.

A careful announcement names the adopted method, preserves ambiguity-set outputs, and ties the target comparison specifically to AsymRouteBench under the stated loss condition.
Does ‘adopt’ itself mean the approach has been deployed everywhere?

No. Here, ‘adopt’ states the design decision in favor of missingness-aware multi-fault factor graphs with ambiguity-set outputs. The decision does not specify a deployment scope, rollout status, or operational result. Those should not be inferred from the word alone.
If an output contains two alternative fault sets, should the decision encourage choosing the shorter one for the final report?

Not merely because it is shorter. The adopted ambiguity-set output exists to preserve alternatives that the observations cannot distinguish. Selecting one as the asserted cause on the basis of presentation preference would undo that part of the decision.

A report can make the alternatives readable while remaining clear that they are alternatives, not one combined set of confirmed concurrent faults and not a secretly preferred single-cause explanation.
Can you phrase the decision in one sentence that includes its reason but no extra claims?

Adopt missingness-aware multi-fault factor graphs with ambiguity-set outputs, because AsymRouteBench reported localization precision and coverage above their respective targets under 30% telemetry loss.

I’d like to turn the adopted approach into a service. The plan is to implement the factor-graph service so it ingests directional paths, models telemetry loss, infers concurrent faults, groups observationally equivalent fault sets, and is validated on AsymRouteBench. How should I describe the plan?

Describe it as planned implementation and validation, not as a service that is already running. The service would take account of directional paths, represent unavailable telemetry without treating it as an observed reading, and infer candidate causal fault sets that may contain concurrent faults. Where the available observations cannot distinguish candidate sets, it would group them as observational equivalents rather than assert a unique cause. Validation on AsymRouteBench is the planned check of that behavior.
What does it mean for the service to ingest directional paths?

It means path information should retain the direction to which it applies. The service should not silently treat a path observed or described in one direction as the path in the reverse direction. That distinction lets the factor graph relate an observation to the path it actually concerns when evaluating a candidate fault set.

The plan does not specify a source or format for path information, or claim that every pair of directions follows different paths.
Why is that an input concern rather than something inference can sort out later?

If directional distinctions are erased on ingestion, inference may be left with observations that appear to concern the same path even when they do not. Keeping the distinction available allows the causal reasoning to use it where relevant.

That does not mean the input alone determines a diagnosis. It means the service should preserve the path context needed to assess whether a proposed fault set could explain the observations.
What should ‘model telemetry loss’ convey in this plan?

It conveys that the service must distinguish unavailable telemetry from telemetry that was observed and had a value. An absent reading should not automatically count as a normal result or as evidence against a candidate fault set.

The plan does not specify why telemetry is missing or say that its absence can never be informative. It calls for loss to be represented in the inference rather than silently ignored or filled in as though the reading were known.
Does that require the service to reconstruct every missing reading?

No. Modeling telemetry loss is not the same as recovering unobserved values. The service can reason from the observations it has while recognizing that unavailable observations may leave some causal explanations unresolved. It should not present an inferred value as though it were a reading that was actually received.
When the plan says ‘infer concurrent faults,’ is it committing to report multiple faults for every incident?

No. It commits to allowing candidate explanations with more than one causal fault. An incident might support a single-fault explanation, a concurrent-fault explanation, or unresolved alternatives; the plan does not predetermine which applies.

The distinction between cause and consequence remains important. Inferring concurrent faults should not mean counting every downstream symptom as an additional fault.
Would the factor graph treat a symptom differently from a candidate fault?

That is the intended causal distinction. A candidate fault belongs to an explanation of the incident; a downstream symptom is something that explanation may account for. The service should compare candidate fault sets against observations without promoting an abnormal observation into a causal fault solely because it is present.

The graph provides a structure for expressing that distinction. It cannot make a disputed causal relationship certain simply by assigning it a label.
What does grouping observational equivalents add after multi-fault inference?

Multi-fault inference makes different fault combinations available as candidate explanations. Grouping observational equivalents addresses what to report when the available observations do not distinguish among those candidates. Without that reporting step, the service might choose one fault set and make the output appear more certain than the evidence permits.

The grouping is about alternatives between candidate sets. It should not be confused with the concurrent faults within any one candidate set.
If two equivalent sets each contain several faults, should the service combine them into one larger set?

Not as an assertion that all those faults occurred. Each candidate set expresses one proposed combination of concurrent faults; observationally equivalent sets express alternative combinations that the observations cannot separate. Their union would make a different causal claim.

The planned output should preserve which faults belong together within an explanation and which explanations remain alternatives.
Does ‘observationally equivalent’ mean the proposed causal situations are identical?

No. It means the available observations do not support distinguishing them for the diagnosis at hand. The proposed fault sets may describe different causal situations. Grouping them acknowledges a limit of the evidence, not an identity between the underlying faults.
How do the directional paths and missing telemetry affect that grouping?

Directional paths determine which observations are relevant to a proposed explanation without assuming that evidence from one direction applies to the other. Telemetry loss limits which of those relevant observations are available. Together, they affect whether the service has grounds to distinguish candidate fault sets.

If a distinction depends on a reading that is unavailable, or on assuming opposite directions share a path, the service should not report the distinction as established merely to produce a single answer.
Could the service still identify a specific fault set when some inputs are missing?

Yes, if the observations that remain support that distinction. The plan does not require an ambiguity group whenever telemetry is incomplete. It requires the service to preserve ambiguity where candidate sets are observationally equivalent, while permitting a more specific result where the available evidence supports it.
What is the role of AsymRouteBench in this implementation plan?

AsymRouteBench is the named validation setting for the planned service. Validation would assess the implemented behavior rather than merely assume that ingesting paths, modeling loss, and running inference produce the intended diagnoses.

This plan does not itself report a validation result for the service. It identifies validation as work to be done.
Should validation check only whether the service produces an output?

No. Producing an output would not show that the service used directional paths appropriately, handled missing telemetry without treating it as an observed value, separated concurrent causal faults from symptoms, or preserved observationally equivalent alternatives. Those are the behaviors the plan is meant to put into practice and that validation should examine.

The plan does not specify a new scoring procedure or report measurements from that validation.
Would it be accurate to say AsymRouteBench has already validated this implemented service?

Not on the basis of this plan. It says to implement the service and validate it on AsymRouteBench. The planned validation should not be described as completed, and the plan supplies no service-specific validation outcome.
I want the output to be useful without hiding uncertainty. How does this plan balance the two?

It aims to infer causal fault sets as specifically as the available directional-path and telemetry evidence allows. When that evidence distinguishes a candidate, the service can express the supported distinction. When several sets are observationally equivalent, grouping them communicates the remaining possibilities without asserting an unsupported single cause.

That also keeps symptoms in their proper role as observations or downstream effects, rather than making the diagnosis look more complete by listing them as additional faults.
Can I describe the planned service as determining the true cause of every incident?

No. The plan allows for concurrent faults, incomplete telemetry, and observationally equivalent explanations. Those conditions can prevent a uniquely supported causal conclusion. A faithful description is that the service will infer candidate causal fault sets and report unresolved alternatives where the observations do not distinguish them.
Could ‘group observational equivalents’ be read as an instruction to group symptoms with faults?

It should not be. The equivalents in this plan are candidate fault sets that cannot be distinguished by the available observations. A downstream symptom may help assess a candidate explanation, but it is not thereby a member of the causal fault set. The service should keep those two roles clear in its output.
What would be a concise implementation statement that preserves all five parts of the plan?

Implement the adopted factor-graph service to ingest directional paths, model telemetry loss, infer concurrent causal faults, group observationally equivalent fault sets in its output, and validate the implemented service on AsymRouteBench.

For this implementation activity, I want to implement PathGraph v1 with separate forward and reverse route dependencies and per-sensor dropout likelihoods for missing telemetry. What should that description convey?

It should convey two specific modeling choices for PathGraph v1. First, dependencies associated with a forward route remain separate from those associated with a reverse route, so the graph does not assume the directions have identical causal relationships. Second, missing telemetry is represented through dropout likelihoods for individual sensors, rather than treating every unavailable reading as an observed value.

“Implement” describes the activity; it does not, by itself, report that PathGraph v1 is finished or that its behavior has been validated.
Why say separate forward and reverse route dependencies instead of just saying the graph supports asymmetric routing?

“Supports asymmetric routing” names the aim, but “separate forward and reverse route dependencies” says what PathGraph v1 is to represent. An observation relevant to a forward-route dependency should not automatically be carried over to a reverse-route dependency, or vice versa.

Separation does not assert that the two routes always differ. It means their dependencies are not made identical by default.
Does ‘dependency’ mean we already know which route caused a particular symptom?

No. A route dependency expresses a modeled relationship that the diagnosis can use when assessing an explanation. It is not, on its own, an observed causal finding about a particular incident.

The important implementation distinction is that the forward and reverse relationships can be represented separately. Whether a particular fault explanation is supported still depends on the observations available for that case.
If the forward and reverse routes happen to coincide, would the separation be misleading?

Not inherently. Representing the directions separately allows them to coincide without assuming that they do. The misleading step would be to force them to share dependencies before the relevant path information supports doing so, or to insist that they differ when it does not.

PathGraph v1’s stated activity is to preserve the directional distinction, not to predetermine the relationship between the routes in every incident.
How should I understand the per-sensor part of the dropout likelihoods?

It means the representation of telemetry dropout is tied to the sensor whose reading is unavailable. The model need not collapse all missing readings into an undifferentiated absence of telemetry. That matters when assessing which potential observations are missing from a candidate explanation.
