The activity does not supply dropout values for any sensor or say how those values are obtained. “Per-sensor” identifies the level at which missingness is represented, not a set of measured rates.
Does a dropout likelihood tell us what the missing sensor would have reported?

No. It concerns the absence of the reading, not the unobserved reading’s value. PathGraph v1 should keep “the sensor did not provide telemetry” distinct from “the sensor provided a normal reading” and from “the sensor provided an abnormal reading.”

Representing dropout can help the inference avoid treating a telemetry gap as a contradiction. It cannot recover the missing observation as a fact.
What if someone reads ‘dropout’ as proof that a fault caused the sensor to stop reporting?

That would add a causal conclusion the activity does not state. A per-sensor dropout likelihood models missing telemetry; it does not, by itself, identify why the telemetry is missing. The diagnosis should not label a network fault as the cause of a gap merely because that gap is represented in the graph.
Are we assuming all the sensors drop out independently?

No independence assumption is specified. Giving sensors their own dropout likelihoods does not establish that their missing readings are independent of one another. The implementation description should not add that claim or infer a particular joint missingness behavior from the phrase “per-sensor.”
Could separate route dependencies and sensor dropout likelihoods conflict with each other?

They address different distinctions. The route dependencies preserve which direction a modeled relationship concerns. The dropout likelihoods preserve whether telemetry from a particular sensor is available. Together, they let PathGraph v1 avoid confusing a gap in direction-relevant evidence with evidence gathered on the opposite direction.

Neither element alone establishes what happened in an incident. They provide a representation in which later inference can respect both direction and missingness.
If telemetry for the forward direction is missing, can the reverse-direction reading fill the gap?

It should not be treated as the missing forward-direction reading merely because it is available. Separate forward and reverse dependencies are meant to prevent that substitution without support. A reverse-direction observation may have its own relevance, but its presence does not turn an unavailable forward-direction observation into an observed one.
Does PathGraph v1 need to say every sensor has missing telemetry?

No. Per-sensor dropout likelihoods let the graph represent the possibility of missing telemetry for sensors; they do not assert that every sensor is missing a reading in every incident. A sensor with an available reading and a sensor without one should remain distinguishable in the diagnosis.
How does this activity relate to keeping faults separate from downstream symptoms?

It supplies part of the context needed for that distinction, without settling it by itself. Directional dependencies help keep an observation tied to the route relationship it may reflect. Dropout likelihoods help prevent an unavailable observation from being mistaken for evidence that a proposed downstream effect did not occur.

PathGraph v1’s stated implementation choices do not themselves identify which conditions are causal faults and which are symptoms. They make it possible to reason about those questions without erasing path direction or telemetry availability.
Could the v1 name be interpreted as saying a particular version has already passed a test?

No. PathGraph v1 is the named version in the implementation activity. The name alone says nothing about completion, testing, performance, or deployment. It is safest to state what is being implemented and avoid attaching an outcome that is not given.
Do we need to specify actual dropout percentages for each sensor in this description?

No percentages are provided for individual sensors in this activity. You can state that PathGraph v1 uses per-sensor dropout likelihoods without inventing their numerical values. The essential point is that missing telemetry is represented at the sensor level, rather than silently treated as an observed reading.
What would be an overstatement about the directional part?

Saying that PathGraph v1 has established that every forward route differs from its reverse route would overstate it. So would saying that separating the dependencies automatically identifies a fault. The activity is to implement separate forward and reverse route dependencies; what any incident’s observations establish is a different question.
And what would be an overstatement about the missingness part?

Saying that the dropout likelihoods reveal every missing reading’s value or its reason for going missing would overstate it. They represent sensor-specific telemetry loss for inference. They should preserve uncertainty where a reading is unavailable, not disguise an unobserved value as a measurement.
Can you give me a compact description of PathGraph v1 that stays strictly within this activity?

Implement PathGraph v1 with distinct dependencies for forward and reverse routes, and per-sensor dropout likelihoods that represent missing telemetry without treating unavailable readings as observed values.
What is the PathGraph v1 artifact at this point?

PathGraph v1 is a module that stores directional route dependencies and sensor dropout likelihoods, and emits factor graphs for multi-fault inference. That describes what the module contains and produces; it does not, by itself, state the outcome of any diagnosis.
What does storing directional route dependencies mean here?

It means the module retains the direction associated with a route dependency. A dependency concerning a forward route need not be treated as the same dependency concerning a reverse route. The artifact preserves that distinction for the factor graphs it emits, without asserting that the routes always differ.
So is PathGraph v1 storing the actual forward and reverse routes for every incident?

The reporting constraint is to avoid presenting one fault as uniquely established when the observations do not support that distinction. The question leaves open how a posterior-set rule should operationalize that constraint.
Would returning an ambiguity set for every incident guarantee the first condition?

It could avoid singleton outputs altogether, but that is not the same as identifying a rule that answers the whole question. It might conceal distinctions that the observations do support, and the question gives no basis for concluding that such outputs would keep held-out coverage above 80%.

A useful rule should preserve ambiguity where it exists without automatically declaring every case ambiguous.
Could the rule abstain instead whenever sets are indistinguishable?

Abstention would avoid asserting an unsupported singleton in those cases. But if abstentions do not qualify as covered incidents, they could reduce held-out coverage. The question does not define the coverage treatment of abstentions or ambiguity-set outputs, so neither strategy can be declared sufficient on its own.
Does keeping coverage above 80% force the rule to make some unsupported unique claims?

That does not follow. Coverage might be maintained through supported unique localizations, qualifying ambiguity-set reports, or some combination, depending on the coverage definition and the held-out incidents. What would count as eliminating unsupported singletons without just renaming them?

In an indistinguishable incident, the output would have to stop asserting a single fault as uniquely causal when the observations cannot support that assertion. It could communicate the unresolved candidate fault sets instead, provided they remain clearly marked as alternatives.

Calling a chosen singleton an “ambiguity set” would not change the substance if the report still conveys that one fault is established. Nor would listing multiple alternatives help if the presentation quietly privileges one as the certain cause.
How does telemetry loss affect the choice of calibration rule?

Missing telemetry can remove observations that might otherwise distinguish candidate fault sets. A posterior-set rule therefore cannot treat an unavailable reading as a normal result or a contradiction merely to justify a singleton. It must base its reporting specificity on what remains observable.

The question does not specify a particular loss percentage for this rule-selection test, so a performance claim under a particular telemetry-loss condition cannot be supplied from the question alone.
Is the rule mainly about choosing between a one-fault and a two-fault explanation?

That can be one kind of unresolved comparison, but the question is broader. Candidate fault sets may differ in membership and may contain one or multiple concurrent faults. The relevant question is whether the available observations warrant selecting one candidate set—or a particular singleton—as the uniquely supported explanation.

A calibration rule should not assume that the shorter explanation is established simply because it contains fewer faults.
Can we select a numerical cutoff now?

The requested answer is a rule that actually meets the joint conditions, not just a plausible-sounding threshold.
What information would distinguish a successful rule from one that merely sounds conservative?

Those are criteria for answering the question, not reported findings about any candidate rule.
Does the question require every ambiguity set to be perfectly calibrated in some broader sense?

No particular posterior-set calibration rule can yet be identified from the stated information. Whether any candidate meets both conditions remains unanswered here.

I want to examine this hypothesis: group observationally equivalent faults before 95% conformal set calibration, so that inference eliminates unsupported singletons while achieving at least 90% localization precision at at least 80% coverage. Is that a careful statement?

That is the reasoning behind the hypothesis, not proof that the ordering will eliminate every unsupported singleton or preserve the stated precision and coverage.
What are we grouping—faults that definitely occurred together?

No. “Observationally equivalent” means the available observations cannot support a distinction between the relevant fault possibilities. Grouping them preserves that uncertainty; it does not assert that every fault appearing in the group occurred.

It is also important to distinguish faults proposed to occur concurrently within one candidate explanation from alternative candidate fault sets that the observations cannot separate. A group of alternatives should not be reported as their union of confirmed causes.
Could two different fault combinations be observationally equivalent?

Yes, conceptually. The available observations might fail to distinguish one candidate combination from another, even though the combinations describe different underlying situations. In that case, grouping should preserve them as alternatives rather than flatten their members into a single larger causal fault set.

The hypothesis does not specify which combinations are equivalent in any particular incident or how many alternatives any group contains.
What does the 95% in ‘95% conformal set calibration’ mean? Is that the expected localization precision?

Are conformal set coverage and incident coverage necessarily the same quantity?

What does ‘eliminate unsupported singletons’ require of the output?

It requires the output not to assert one fault as the uniquely supported cause when the observations leave relevant fault alternatives indistinguishable. In those cases, the unresolved alternatives should remain visible in the reported set rather than be reduced to a single-fault claim.

It does not prohibit every singleton. Where the observations do support a unique single-fault explanation, a singleton need not be unsupported. The proposed elimination concerns the unsupported ones.
If a calibration rule picks the highest-scoring fault within an equivalence group, has it solved the ambiguity?

Not merely by picking it. A ranking can favor one candidate without making the available observations distinguish that candidate as uniquely causal. If the report then asserts the selected fault alone, it may recreate the unsupported singleton the hypothesis is meant to eliminate.

The hypothesis calls for retaining the observational equivalence through calibration and reporting, not simply giving an unresolved choice a numerical winner.
Could the calibrated result contain only one group without being an unsupported singleton?

Yes. One reported group is not necessarily one asserted fault. That group might contain alternatives that remain observationally equivalent. The report should make clear whether it is identifying a uniquely supported causal fault or identifying a group within which the evidence cannot choose.

Likewise, reporting one candidate fault set that contains concurrent faults is different from reporting one individual fault. Counting or judging unsupported singletons requires those distinctions to remain clear.
Would grouping everything into one enormous set satisfy the hypothesis?

Not on that fact alone. It might avoid choosing unsupported single faults, but it would not establish at least 90% localization precision or at least 80% incident coverage. Nor would indiscriminate grouping reflect the stated idea of grouping *observationally equivalent* faults: equivalence depends on what the observations cannot distinguish, not merely on a desire to avoid specific claims.

The hypothesis predicts both restraint and useful localization. Neither should be inferred simply from producing large sets.
Could the set calibration itself tell us which faults are downstream symptoms?

The hypothesis does not say that it can. Calibration of sets concerns how the proposed outputs are formed or qualified; it does not automatically determine whether a condition is a causal fault or a downstream symptom. An observed symptom should not become an alternative causal fault just because it appears among diagnostic candidates.

For this hypothesis, the immediate claim is about grouping observational equivalents before calibration, eliminating unsupported singletons, and meeting the stated precision and coverage thresholds.
Does the hypothesis claim there will be no errors at all?

No. Eliminating unsupported singletons is a specific predicted outcome, not a claim of perfect diagnosis. The precision threshold is at least 90%, not 100%, and the coverage threshold is at least 80%, not every incident. The hypothesis should not be paraphrased as universal correctness.
If the measured precision were exactly 90%, would that meet the stated precision threshold?

Yes. “At least 90%” includes exactly 90%, as well as values above it. Likewise, exactly 80% would meet the hypothesis’s “at least 80% coverage” threshold. The absence of unsupported singletons remains a separate part of the predicted outcome; meeting the two numerical thresholds alone would not establish it.
Does eliminating unsupported singletons automatically keep coverage at or above 80%?

No. Changing unique claims to ambiguity-set outputs could affect how many incidents qualify as covered, depending on the evaluation definition. The hypothesis predicts that unsupported singletons can be eliminated *while* coverage remains at least 80%; it does not make that coexistence automatic.

The same caution applies to precision. A rule's effect on one measure cannot simply be assumed to establish the others.
Could a calibrated ambiguity set count as a covered incident?

That depends on what qualifies as a covered diagnostic output, which this hypothesis does not define. An ambiguity set can convey meaningful localization without asserting a unique fault, but it should not be silently scored as a uniquely resolved incident.

To interpret the at-least-80% coverage claim, the treatment of such outputs would need to be clear. No particular treatment or measured coverage follows from the hypothesis alone.
Should I say the 95% calibration guarantees that no indistinguishable incident receives a singleton?

No. The nominal 95% level does not itself guarantee the specific behavior of eliminating unsupported singletons. That behavior is an explicit part of the hypothesis about grouping before calibration and how the resulting sets are reported. It remains to be established, not inferred from the number 95%.
What would be the substantive failure if a grouped output still described one member as the cause?

If that member is observationally indistinguishable from other alternatives, asserting it as the cause would undo the point of grouping. For the hypothesis to hold, the output must preserve unresolved alternatives in substance, not just include them somewhere in a list.
How do we distinguish an unsupported singleton from a legitimate one without assuming that any multi-fault story is correct?

The distinction rests on whether the available observations support a unique single-fault explanation. If they do not separate that explanation from a different fault set—including one with concurrent faults—the singleton is unsupported as a unique conclusion. That does not prove the multi-fault alternative occurred; it means the evidence cannot justify selecting the singleton alone.

If the observations do distinguish the alternatives and support one fault, a singleton could be legitimate. The hypothesis is about respecting that evidential boundary.
Is this a statement about a particular percentage of telemetry loss?

No telemetry-loss percentage is specified in this hypothesis. It names the 95% conformal set-calibration level and the performance targets of at least 90% precision and at least 80% coverage, but it does not attach those claims to a stated loss rate. Adding a particular loss percentage to this hypothesis would extend its wording.

Hypothesis: grouping observationally equivalent faults before 95% conformal set calibration will eliminate unsupported singleton fault claims while achieving at least 90% localization precision at at least 80% incident coverage.

I propose using observability-stratified conformal thresholds and equivalence-class safeguards to target at least 90% localization precision, at least 80% incident coverage, and zero unsupported singletons. How should I describe the idea?

Describe it as a proposed reporting and calibration approach, not an achieved result. Observability-stratified conformal thresholds would allow the calibration rule to account for differences in how much relevant evidence is available. Equivalence-class safeguards would prevent the output from singling out a fault when the observations leave fault alternatives indistinguishable.

What does ‘observability-stratified’ mean without committing to particular strata?

It means the thresholding approach would take account of differences in available observations, rather than treating every incident as equally observable. An incident with missing relevant telemetry may support a different degree of diagnostic specificity from one with more relevant evidence.

The proposal does not define how many strata there are, how they are assigned, or what threshold applies to any stratum. Those details should not be presented as decisions already made.
Is the proposal saying that less observable incidents should always get larger output sets?

No such rule is specified. Less available evidence can make distinctions harder to support, but the actual diagnostic output depends on what the remaining observations distinguish. Observability-stratified thresholds are proposed as a way to account for differing evidence conditions; they are not, by themselves, a fixed instruction about set size in every incident.
Why use conformal thresholds here rather than just always output the highest-ranked fault?

A highest-ranked fault is not necessarily a uniquely supported fault. Thresholded set reporting offers a way to retain alternatives when a unique claim would exceed what the observations establish. The equivalence-class safeguard addresses that point directly: candidates that cannot be observationally distinguished should not be reduced to one asserted cause merely because the system ranks one first.

That explains the proposed rationale. It does not show that any particular conformal threshold attains the three targets.
What exactly is an equivalence-class safeguard safeguarding?

It safeguards the distinction between a supported unique localization and an unresolved choice among observationally equivalent fault explanations. If the available observations cannot separate the alternatives, the output should preserve that equivalence rather than assert an unsupported singleton.

An equivalence class represents unresolved alternatives, not a declaration that every fault appearing in those alternatives occurred.
Could an equivalence class contain candidate sets with concurrent faults?

Yes, conceptually. A candidate fault set may propose concurrent causes, and multiple candidate sets may remain observationally indistinguishable. The safeguard should keep those levels separate: faults within one candidate set are proposed together; different candidate sets are alternative explanations.

The proposal does not specify which sets would be equivalent in any particular incident.
Does ‘zero unsupported singletons’ mean no single-fault reports at all?

No. A single-fault report can be appropriate when the available observations support that fault as a unique causal explanation. Could the system satisfy the zero target by declining to answer whenever there is ambiguity?

Declining to assert a singleton in an ambiguous case would avoid that particular error, but it would not establish ≥80% incident coverage. Whether an abstention or an ambiguity-set report qualifies as a covered output is not specified here.

The proposal targets all three outcomes together. Avoiding unsupported singletons cannot simply be assumed to preserve coverage or precision.
What if it always reports a large collection of possible faults instead?

That would not automatically meet the proposal either. A large collection may avoid a unique assertion, but it does not establish ≥90% localization precision or ≥80% incident coverage. It could also obscure the difference between concurrent faults within a candidate explanation and alternative explanations.

The safeguard is meant to retain alternatives that are observationally equivalent, not to group possibilities indiscriminately.
How do observability-stratified thresholds and equivalence-class safeguards work together conceptually?

The thresholds would govern how the diagnostic set is selected in light of the available evidence, with observability taken into account. The safeguard would constrain the specificity of the resulting report: if selecting or presenting a set would break an unresolved observational equivalence and assert a single fault, that output would not be acceptable as a supported singleton.

Their roles are complementary, but the proposal does not specify an algorithm for combining them or prove that their combination meets the targets.
Could a threshold alone guarantee zero unsupported singletons?

Not from what is stated here. A threshold might determine which candidates appear in an output, but the unsupported-singleton question also depends on whether the observations actually distinguish alternatives and on what the report asserts. That is why the proposal names equivalence-class safeguards separately.

No particular threshold or guarantee has been supplied.
Does stratifying by observability mean treating missing telemetry as evidence that a fault was absent?

No. Observability concerns what evidence is available to support a distinction. Missing telemetry should remain different from an observed reading that contradicts a candidate explanation. Stratifying by observability should not turn an unavailable observation into proof that a fault or downstream effect did not occur.
Where does asymmetric routing fit into this proposal?

It remains part of the diagnosis context: observations associated with one direction need not describe the reverse direction. What counts as relevant available evidence, and whether fault explanations are observationally equivalent, should not depend on an unsupported assumption that the two paths are identical.

The proposal does not claim that asymmetric routing has a particular measured effect on these thresholds, nor does it specify particular paths.
And does the safeguard help keep downstream symptoms out of the causal fault set?

The diagnosis still needs to distinguish causal faults from downstream symptoms. An equivalence-class safeguard should operate on candidate causal explanations without treating an observed downstream effect as another fault merely to fill out an output set.

But the proposal does not supply a separate symptom-rejection measurement or establish that the safeguard, on its own, correctly classifies every symptom.
How should I read the precision and coverage targets together?

You would need information about which sensors were unavailable together, with their directional relevance retained. And what more would I need before saying that correlation explains the coverage outcome?

You would need to connect the joint gaps to the incidents that lack qualifying outputs and to the fault-set distinctions those gaps might have affected. Even an observed association between joint dropout and uncovered incidents would not automatically establish causation: the same incidents might be difficult to localize for other reasons.

The question does not establish that this pattern occurred. It illustrates why directional relevance, rather than just the number of missing sensors, matters.
Would those gaps necessarily create ambiguity between fault sets?

No. Other available observations might still distinguish the candidate explanations. Joint dropout can remove potentially useful evidence, but it does not make every affected incident ambiguous. Whether an incident remains distinguishable depends on what the remaining observations support.

Not necessarily. An ambiguity-set output may still qualify as a covered diagnosis, depending on the coverage definition and what the set communicates. Keep ‘no telemetry was available’ separate from ‘telemetry was available and showed no effect.’ Even if several sensors drop out together, their absence does not demonstrate that a predicted symptom failed to occur. They are intended to represent linked missingness: relevant sensor readings may become unavailable together. That differs from looking only at each sensor’s dropout separately. Why track precision if worst-seed coverage is the main concern?

Coverage tells us how broadly qualifying diagnostic outputs are produced. Precision concerns the correctness of the localization claims those outputs make. What exactly is the singleton rate supposed to measure?

I propose adding budgeted directional probes, chosen to distinguish concurrent fault sets from downstream symptoms. If the evidence remains insufficient, the diagnosis should retain ambiguity sets. How should I describe that proposal?

Describe it as a proposed way to seek additional, direction-relevant evidence without assuming that probing will resolve every incident. The probes would be chosen for their potential to distinguish competing causal fault sets from one another and from explanations in which an observed condition is a downstream symptom. “Budgeted” means probe selection is constrained, though the proposal gives no numerical budget or selection rule. If the resulting evidence is still insufficient, the output should preserve the unresolved fault alternatives as an ambiguity set rather than assert a unique cause.
What makes a probe ‘directional’ in this proposal?

Its evidence must be interpreted with respect to the direction it concerns. Under asymmetric routing, a probe relevant to one direction cannot automatically be taken as evidence about an identical reverse path. The proposal does not name particular paths or probe types; it requires direction to remain part of how a probe is chosen and interpreted.
Would we have to probe both directions every time?

No such requirement is stated. The proposal is to choose budgeted directional probes that may resolve a relevant distinction. Whether one direction, the other, or neither offers a useful distinction depends on the candidate explanations and available evidence. A fixed rule to probe both directions would be an additional decision.
What is the budget constraining?

It constrains the use of probes, so the approach cannot assume unlimited additional observations. The proposal does not specify the budget’s units, size, or allocation. Its substantive point is that probes should be chosen for their potential diagnostic value under a constraint, rather than added without regard to whether they distinguish anything.
Does ‘chosen to distinguish’ mean we already know what each probe will show?

No. It means choosing a probe because different possible outcomes could bear differently on competing explanations. The actual result remains unknown until a probe is performed. Even afterward, its observation might be uninformative, unavailable, or compatible with more than one fault set; selecting a probe does not guarantee a unique diagnosis.
How can a probe help separate concurrent faults from a downstream symptom?

The diagnosis may have one candidate explanation in which multiple faults are causal and another in which an observed condition follows downstream from a different fault set. A useful probe would seek evidence relevant to a distinction between those explanations, rather than merely repeat an observation both already explain.

That is a general account of its purpose, not a claim that a particular probe or result proves one interpretation. If the resulting observation is compatible with both, the cause-versus-symptom distinction remains unresolved.
Does the proposal assume that there is only one causal fault once the symptom is excluded?

No. Excluding a downstream symptom from the causal fault set does not require reducing the explanation to one fault. Multiple causal faults may occur concurrently. The probes are intended to help tell those concurrent causes apart from their effects, not to impose a single-cause account.
When you say ‘fault sets,’ do the members of a set all represent alternatives?

Not necessarily. Within a candidate fault set, the members can be proposed as concurrent causes. Different candidate sets can be alternative explanations. An ambiguity set preserves candidate explanations that the evidence still cannot distinguish; it should not be flattened into a claim that every fault mentioned across those alternatives occurred.
Could a probe distinguish two candidate fault sets while still leaving it unclear whether another observation is a symptom?

Yes. Resolving one comparison need not resolve every causal relationship in an incident. The report should reflect the distinction actually supported by the new evidence and preserve uncertainty about any cause-versus-symptom question that remains open. A probe result should not be used as permission to make unrelated causal claims.
How should incomplete telemetry affect the choice of probes?

It makes the remaining evidential gaps relevant to selection. A probe can be considered for whether its possible observations would help distinguish explanations left unresolved by missing telemetry. But a telemetry gap is not itself an observed negative result, and the proposal does not say that probes can recover the missing readings or must be aimed at any particular sensor.
If a directional probe returns no usable observation, can the system treat that as ruling out a fault?

Not merely because no usable observation was obtained. An unavailable probe result is different from a usable result that bears against a candidate explanation. If the evidence remains insufficient, the proposal says to retain the ambiguity set rather than manufacture a distinction from the absence of a reading.
What if the probe does produce an observation but both candidate sets predict it?

Then that observation may add context without distinguishing those sets. The diagnosis should not call a candidate uniquely supported solely because a probe was performed. The ambiguity set remains appropriate wherever the combined evidence still fails to separate the alternatives.
Would a probe aimed at confirming the most likely fault be enough?

Only if its possible outcomes could also distinguish that fault explanation from the relevant alternatives. An observation compatible with the favored fault but equally compatible with other candidate sets would not justify selecting it as the sole cause. The proposal prioritizes discriminating evidence, not simply more evidence consistent with an existing preference.
Can a probe be useful without yielding a single fault as the answer?

Yes, conceptually. It might rule out some candidate explanations while leaving others observationally indistinguishable. The resulting ambiguity set could be more restricted without becoming a unique diagnosis. The proposal allows the report to communicate that narrower but still unresolved conclusion.
Does ‘retain ambiguity sets’ mean the system should always keep the same alternatives even after probing?

No. New evidence may distinguish some alternatives, so the set of unresolved explanations may change. ‘Retain’ means not discarding ambiguity that the available evidence still cannot resolve. It does not require preserving candidates contradicted by usable evidence, and it does not imply that every probe will change the reported set.
Could we use the budget to keep probing until one explanation is left?

The proposal does not promise that a unique explanation will be reachable within the budget, or even with more observations. The budget limits probing, while the reporting rule handles the case in which evidence remains insufficient. Choosing a single explanation just because probing stops would turn a resource limit into an unsupported causal conclusion.
What does the proposal say about how to choose among candidate probes?

It gives the purpose of selection: seek direction-relevant probes capable of distinguishing concurrent fault sets from downstream symptoms, subject to a budget. It does not specify a ranking formula, a particular probe menu, or a tie-breaking rule. Those details should remain open rather than being presented as part of the proposal.
Could a probe from the reverse direction stand in for evidence missing from the forward direction?

Not automatically. It may provide information about the reverse direction, but asymmetric routing means that information need not describe the forward path. Its diagnostic value depends on whether it actually distinguishes the candidate explanations under consideration, not on an assumption that the directions are interchangeable.
Does this proposal claim the probes will improve localization precision or incident coverage?

No measured improvement is stated. The proposal describes an additional way to seek discriminating evidence under a probe budget while preserving honest ambiguity when that evidence is insufficient. Whether adding those probes changes any performance measure would require evaluation; it is not an outcome contained in the proposal.
Should a downstream symptom ever appear in the diagnostic output?

It can appear as an observation or a consequence being explained, but it should not be asserted as a causal fault merely because it is visible. The proposed probes aim to help distinguish those roles. If they fail to resolve the distinction, the output should make that uncertainty clear rather than promote the symptom into a confirmed fault.
If probing makes one candidate fault set more plausible but does not rule out an observationally indistinguishable alternative, may the report still choose the first?

It may describe what the evidence supports, but it should not assert a unique causal fault set if the relevant alternatives remain indistinguishable on the available observations. A ranking and a justified unique diagnosis are different claims. The ambiguity-set rule is meant to prevent that gap from being hidden by a decisive-sounding output.
Does budgeting the probes weaken that reporting rule?

No. A limited budget can explain why further evidence was not sought, but it cannot make unresolved alternatives distinguishable. Once the available probe evidence and other observations are considered, any remaining uncertainty should still be reported as an ambiguity set rather than an unsupported single cause.
Can you give me one sentence that captures the proposal without inventing probe settings or promising a result?

Add budgeted, direction-relevant probes selected for their potential to distinguish concurrent causal fault sets from downstream symptoms, while retaining ambiguity sets whenever the resulting evidence is insufficient to support a unique fault explanation.

The plan is to implement entropy-guided directional probes, limited to three per incident, and evaluate precision, coverage, and ambiguity reporting under 30% telemetry loss. How should I describe it?

Describe it as an implementation and evaluation plan, not an achieved result: implement directional probes selected using an entropy-guided criterion, allow no more than three probes per incident, and evaluate localization precision, incident coverage, and ambiguity reporting under 30% telemetry loss. What does ‘entropy-guided’ mean without claiming we have settled the selection algorithm?

Conceptually, it means choosing probes with the aim of reducing uncertainty among candidate diagnostic explanations. The plan does not identify the exact uncertainty quantity, how expected changes are calculated, or a rule for choosing among probes with similar value.

No. A probe is selected before its result is known, and the resulting observation may not separate the candidate fault sets. Entropy guidance is a proposed basis for selecting limited additional observations, not a guarantee of a unique or correct diagnosis.

Because evidence about one direction need not describe the other under asymmetric routing. A directional probe should be interpreted in relation to the direction it concerns, rather than silently treating a forward-path observation as a reverse-path observation or vice versa. The plan does not name particular paths or require the directions to differ in every incident.
Does the plan require probing both forward and reverse directions?

No. It calls for directional probes and limits their number, but does not prescribe how probes are distributed between directions. Their selection should remain tied to the diagnostic distinctions they could inform, without assuming a fixed number for either direction.
What exactly does ‘limited to three per incident’ mean?

It sets a maximum of three probes for each incident, not a requirement to issue exactly three. The plan leaves open whether fewer probes are appropriate for a particular incident. It does not specify timing, the number of possible probe candidates, or another resource budget.
Could we issue a fourth probe if the first three leave the diagnosis ambiguous?

Not within this plan’s stated limit. Does running only one probe count as failing to use the budget?

No. A maximum is a constraint, not a usage target. The plan does not say that using more probes is always better. How should the probe-selection idea handle concurrent faults?

It should allow candidate explanations that contain more than one causal fault. Choosing a probe does not establish in advance which explanation is true.

The plan does not make an abnormal observation a causal fault merely by using it in probe selection. Candidate causal faults and downstream symptoms must remain different kinds of claims. A probe can be sought to inform that distinction, but its result must be interpreted against the causal alternatives; the existence of a symptom alone does not justify adding a fault.
Suppose one probe result is compatible with both a concurrent-fault explanation and a downstream-symptom explanation. What then?

That result would not, on its own, resolve the distinction. The diagnosis could consider any other available evidence and, within the limit of three probes per incident, whether another directional probe might distinguish the alternatives. If they remain observationally indistinguishable, the report should preserve the unresolved fault-set alternatives rather than assert one causal story.
Does a failed or unavailable probe result count as evidence against a candidate fault set?

Not merely because no usable result was obtained. An unavailable probe observation is different from an observed result that contradicts a candidate explanation. Under incomplete telemetry, that distinction remains important: a missing value cannot be treated as a known normal or abnormal reading simply to narrow the diagnosis.

It is the condition under which the planned evaluation of precision, coverage, and ambiguity reporting will take place. It does not mean 30% of incidents are excluded, identify which readings are lost in a specific incident, or state whether any particular probe result will be unavailable. No. A directional probe may provide an additional observation, but it should not be described as reconstructing every missing reading or revealing what unavailable sensors would have reported. The evaluation remains under the stated 30% telemetry-loss condition; probing is a proposed way to seek discriminating evidence within a three-per-incident limit.
Why evaluate precision and coverage separately?

Precision concerns the correctness of fault-localization claims; incident coverage concerns how many incidents receive qualifying diagnostic outputs. More probing could affect either measure, but an improvement in one cannot be assumed to establish an improvement in the other. The plan calls for evaluating both without stating their eventual values.
Does ‘coverage’ mean a probe returns a measurement in that percentage of cases?

Not here. In this diagnosis context, coverage concerns incidents receiving qualifying diagnostic outputs; it is not a stated probe-response rate. The plan does not define how ambiguous reports qualify for incident coverage, so the eventual evaluation would need to make that interpretation clear.
What should the ambiguity-reporting evaluation look for conceptually?

It should examine whether reports preserve fault-set alternatives when the available observations, including any probe results, cannot distinguish them. A report should not describe one candidate as the uniquely established cause just because a probe was attempted or the per-incident limit was reached. The plan does not prescribe a numerical ambiguity metric or provide a result on that behavior.

Reporting those alternatives is not the same as asserting the union of all their faults occurred. That distinction matters when evaluating whether probing improved localization without hiding uncertainty.

Does the selector have to test forward and reverse paths equally?
